title: 4. The Third Method of Correlative Thinking — Empathy (共感)
content:
### 4.1. The Meaning of Empathic Thinking: The Universal Engine the West Borrowed and Used to Change the World

In Chapter 3, through Buddhist mythos (circulation), we confirmed that all things in heaven and earth are tightly bound in "relationship" as a single vast organic web. But the mere realization that all things are connected cannot, in practice, control the conflicts and threats of reality (especially the ethical tasks of artificial intelligence). Within the connected web of relationships, we must discern what is right and wrong, distinguish good from evil (善惡), and erect a clear order (Logos). For this reason, thought, passing necessarily through Daoism and Buddhism, moves on to the thinking of Chapter 3 [Part I's third method], empathy (共感)—which is completed upon the Confucian foundation of ethical standards and social responsibility.

We usually regard "empathy" as no more than a private disposition that emotionally sympathizes with another's sorrow. But from the perspective of world history, empathy (sympathy/empathy) was the engine of a great revolution that shook the world (Hwang Tae-yeon, 2023). The Enlightenment thinkers of Europe (Leibniz, Voltaire, and others) translated and actively interpreted the Confucianism of the East—especially the concepts of "benevolence (仁)," which regards others as one's own body, and "reciprocity (恕, putting oneself in another's place)." On this basis they toppled the divine right of kings and invented the modern universal human right that "all human beings are equal, rational beings capable of empathizing with one another," transforming the West and the whole world. Yet the East itself failed to realize how cosmic and modern a thought its own Confucianism was—one capable of toppling the pre-modern. That is, genuine empathy at the level of Logos was the most powerful civilizational blueprint for reorganizing human society ethically and horizontally.

Empathy makes it so that even the same words can be received entirely differently depending on the listener's situation. Saying only "it's okay" to a friend who failed an exam, and saying "next time let's prepare together" after listening fully to their heart, carry different weight. Empathy is precisely this power to read the temperature of a relationship.

AI can imitate the expression of emotion, but the subject that actually performs responsible empathy is still the human. So empathy is a human ability that becomes more precious, not less, as technology advances.

The third stage, "empathy (共感)," signifies the ability to deeply empathize with others, to resonate, and to form strong communal bonds. It is the process of understanding and sharing another's emotions to draw out mutual connection and support. In the AI era, the human must shift from an isolated "rational agent" to a "relational being" rooted in community, through a model of "the economy of empathy" grounded in the awareness of "I-Here-Now." Such an economy values connection and the present moment, and it highlights humanity's distinctive strength in that AI cannot experience genuine empathy. The human is healed and finds meaning through "story and communal connection." Storytelling is itself a "correlative act" that creates meaning and promotes connection, especially when shared empathically.

A new human ontology sees the human as the "human as a connecting being" who builds bridges between ideas, between times, and between people. The traditional Korean value of "*jeong* (情)," when combined with modern innovation, can suggest a healthier social path. Because AI can imitate emotion but cannot truly "feel" or experience "qualia," the human's genuine capacity for empathy becomes an irreplaceable asset.

"Empathy" functions not as a mere "soft skill" but as a fundamental economic and social organizing principle of the AI era. As AI handles analytic tasks, human labor will increasingly concentrate on empathy-rich activities such as care, connection, and community-building. This means a revaluation of the "yin (陰)" aspect of the economy and society—relational value—which is currently often undervalued. The success of this "empathy economy" depends on powerful "social capital" such as trust and goodwill.

The act of shared storytelling and narrative-building is a powerful and distinctively human mechanism for creating collective meaning and resilience, essential for navigating the anxiety and uncertainty of the AI transition. Story transforms "isolated, chaotic events" into a "meaningful, coherent sequence." But story must be followed by the practice of empathy. AI can generate text, but it cannot participate in the shared, embodied, empathic process of meaning-making. The emphasis on "empathy" requires a revaluation of leadership and power, demanding a shift from a hierarchical command-and-control model to a more relational, empathic, and facilitative style. Leadership grounded in wisdom and empathy becomes important. This stands in contrast to the traditional power structures associated with a credentialist society.

### 4.2. Confucian Logos (儒敎)

We have confirmed that empathy was the hidden driving force that led Western modernization, and a powerful tool that breaks artificial measures. But the more the intelligent-information age is thrown into extreme confusion by pluralism, the more paradoxically a firmer measure of good and evil and a transparent social standard are needed. This is why we must once again, urgently, summon a cool-headed, ethical Confucian Logos beyond compassionate pity.

This sentence, unlike the two preceding propositions, clearly erects boundaries. It is the attitude that says a given thing is what it is (X), and what is not is not (–X). This can be understood not as erasing differences, but as a thinking that seeks to set each in its proper place and role.

Take the school as an example: the responsibility of the teacher and that of the student differ. A joke and violence between friends differ, and help and interference differ. If everything is said to be "more or less the same," the community in fact collapses. Logos emphasizes this ethics of distinction.

Therefore "X is X, and –X is –X" does not mean exclusivity alone. It means that properly calling each being by its name and role is the starting point of order and respect.

Confucian Logos is a way of thinking that seeks to realize a harmonious social order by rightly setting the principle (理) and the designation (名) of things, and by fulfilling the way (道) according to each one's role and relationship. Regarding friend (X) and enemy (–X), Confucianism, unlike Daoism and Buddhism, says "X is X, and –X is –X." That is, unlike Daoism—which says the enemy (–X) is a friend (X) and so love your enemy—or Buddhism—which says there is neither friend (X) nor enemy (–X)—Confucianism says the friend is the friend and the enemy is the enemy. The proposition "X is X, and –X is –X" means that each being must be faithful to its own essence and role (X) and must be clearly distinguished from what is not (–X). In Confucianism, the ruler must be ruler-like and the minister minister-like; study must be learned and practiced; a friend must come from afar; and one must revere one's own near parents above the distant parents of others. This reflects the perspective of the rectification of names (正名論): that each member of society can form an orderly, stable community by knowing and practicing what they ought to do from their own position.

#### 4.2.1. The Reinterpretation of Benevolence (仁): A New Relational Ethics

Benevolence (仁) is, in Confucianism, the core of being human—simply put, "the heart that regards the other as oneself." With benevolence, one cannot simply pass by the suffering of another. This heart is still—indeed, all the more—needed in the AI era. When an AI algorithm produces a result that disadvantages a particular group, without the sense of benevolence that asks, upon seeing that result, "what would it have been like had I been in that position?", the injustice goes unseen.

When the Logos principle that X is X and –X is –X combines with benevolence (仁), the relational ethics of the AI era is completed: "acknowledge difference, but difference must not become discrimination." Men and women differ (X ≠ –X), old and young differ, the disabled and the non-disabled differ—but ensuring that this difference does not lead to unfair discrimination within AI systems is the AI ethics of benevolence. To apply the sense of benevolence in the process of designing and reviewing AI systems means to examine results from the standpoint of everyone the algorithm affects.

Benevolence (仁), the core idea of Confucianism, is the essence of being human and the foundation of all relational ethics. Benevolence (仁) is grounded in love and care for others—that is, empathy and the heart of commiseration (惻隱之心)—and offers important guidance for establishing a new relational ethics, in the AI era, between human and human and between human and AI. AI can imitate human emotion, but the true heart of benevolence (仁)—the ethical subjectivity that empathizes with the suffering of others and voluntarily does good—is a domain distinctive to the human. Therefore the relational ethics of the AI era must clearly distinguish the roles of the human (X) and AI (–X) (X ≠ –X) and must emphasize the human's ethical responsibility to guide AI toward promoting human dignity and the good (善) of the community.

#### 4.2.2. Overcoming the "*Han* (恨)" of Technological Alienation

Benevolence (仁), the core idea of Confucianism, advances—in comparing the human and AI—to the concept of *han* (恨), distinctive to the human alone. *Han* (恨) is an emotion distinctive to Korea that is hard to translate simply. It is not mere sorrow or anger but a deep emotional state in which long-unresolved injustice and longing are intermingled. In the AI era, a new form of *han* is arising. The benefits of technology concentrate among a few, and many people who cannot keep pace with the speed of digital transformation are left behind in alienation and deprivation. Rural elders, the middle-aged unfamiliar with digital devices, young people doing platform labor as irregular workers—these bear the new *han* (恨) of the AI era.

Korean culture has the wisdom of resolving *han* not by merely suppressing it or letting it explode, but through "*hanpuri* (the release of *han*)." From the perspective of *hwajaeng*, the *hanpuri* of technological alienation is the institutional effort to invite alienated groups as participants in the AI era. Expanding digital education opportunities; intergenerational technology-sharing programs in which the old and the young take part together; governance in which the local community together chooses and uses AI technology—such practices are the way of releasing the *han* of technological alienation through *hwajaeng*.

The rapid advance of AI technology brings convenience and abundance to some classes, but on the other hand it can cause technological alienation through job loss, the deepening of the digital divide, and so on. Such alienation can leave a deep "*han* (恨)" in the individual and in society as a whole. The communal thought of Confucianism aims to overcome such technological alienation and to orient toward a community of mutual flourishing (相生) in which all prosper together. This means building an inclusive social system in which the benefits of AI development are distributed evenly across society as a whole, in which a social safety net is built so that no one is alienated by technology, and in which all members can participate in the process of technological development and share its fruits—and this too is a domain distinctive to the human.

The following table compares the theories of empathy/postulate in Western philosophy (Kant, Hegel) and Eastern thought (Confucius, Buddhism). Kant may be compared with Buddhism, Hegel with Confucianism.

**Table 4-1. Comparison of Western Philosophy (Kant) and Eastern Thought (Buddhism)**

| Category | Kant (West) | Buddhism (East) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moral principle | • Emphasis on the sense of duty and rational ought • Help through compassion is not regarded as morality • "Postulates" for realizing the highest good (immortality of the soul, freedom, God) | • The thought of dependent arising (緣起) and emptiness (空) • Compassion (慈悲) and non-self (無我) — the mutual connectedness of all beings |
| Concept of empathy | • Emphasis on moral action grounded in "duty" and "respect" rather than direct "empathy" • "Postulate" is a concept arising from the necessity of practical reason | • A practical attitude of empathizing with and relieving the suffering of others through "compassion" • Enhancing empathy by understanding that all people are changing beings • The ease of conflict resolution |
| Implications for the AI era | • Considering AI's non-emotional character, the need to explore the limits of human "rational ethics" and transcendent value • The importance of setting "regulative principles" for the problem of AI's judgmental bias | • Highlighting the importance of "relational intelligence" and "interdependence" in the AI era • A survival strategy through "spiritual transcendence" and "inner reflection," acknowledging AI's incompleteness |

**Table 4-2. Comparison of Western Philosophy (Hegel) and Eastern Thought (Confucius)**

| Category | Hegel (West) | Confucius (East) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moral principle | • Dialectical self-realization (thesis-antithesis-synthesis) • Sees contradiction as the driving force of development • Stages of ethical life (family, civil society, state) | • Emphasis on moral virtues such as benevolence (仁) and propriety (禮) • Self-completion through self-cultivation (修身) • Emphasis on self-reflection and practice |
| Concept of empathy | • Through "love," overcoming isolated existence and forming a unified self-consciousness of self and other • Reflection on relationship through the dialectical process | • As the core of "benevolence (仁)," containing the capacity for empathy such as "the heart of commiseration" • Possessing a system that projects the meaning of others through "empathy" |
| Implications for the AI era | • Understanding the "contradictory relationship" of AI and the human as a "driving force of development" • Emphasizing "holistic" problem-solving ability through collaboration with AI • The importance of "relational" understanding and "communication" for AI-era leadership | • Re-emphasizing "empathy" and "character education" as the core of "humanity" in the AI era • A leadership of the "warm heart" and "empathic power" that AI cannot replace |

### 4.3. The Art of Relationship, *Beomjeol* (凡節)

We have confirmed that Confucian Logos is a universal measure and ethical framework that reconstructs humanity. This macroscopic philosophical foundation must not remain a matter of grasping at clouds; it must live and breathe as concrete manners and institutions in our daily life. The practical etiquette and norms of a new age—in which AI agents and humans will live in daily collision—that is, "*beomjeol* (凡節)"—are now newly designed.

Logos connects to *beomjeol*. This is, in every case, a domain distinctive to the human, who has a body. *Beomjeol* (凡節) refers to the etiquette and norms that smoothly maintain relationships among people. In the AI era, a new form of *beomjeol* is needed. Whether to turn the camera on in a video conference; whether one may submit AI-written text as one's own; whether one must obtain permission when posting another's photograph on social media—in such new situations, society must together decide what counts as polite conduct.

The core of AI etiquette is transparency. Not passing on AI-generated information without verifying its source; not using AI to manipulate or deceive others—this is the basis of AI-era *beomjeol*. The principle at the core of Confucian Logos, "call names rightly (正名)," remains valid in the AI era.

*Beomjeol* (凡節) signifies the etiquette and social norms of daily life, an essential element for smooth human relations and harmonious communal living. As AI enters deeply into human life, new norms and etiquette for the interaction between human and AI—that is, "the *beomjeol* of the AI era"—are becoming necessary.

#### 4.3.1. Defining Roles and Responsibilities

In the AI era, not only the relationship between human and human but also the setting of the relationship between human and AI emerges as an important task. It is necessary to clearly define the scope of AI's role and capability and the locus of responsibility for AI's actions. The human, as the subject who develops and uses AI, must bear ethical responsibility, and AI must be used, under human control and supervision, in the direction of promoting human welfare. Moreover, the human must make efforts to prevent the misunderstandings and conflicts that may arise in interaction with AI, and to form a healthy relationship grounded in mutual respect and understanding.

#### 4.3.2. The Reconstruction of Trust: Empathy Capital

Trust is the invisible glue that makes society run smoothly. When people trust one another, transaction costs fall, cooperation becomes easier, and creative attempts become possible. In the AI era, this trust faces new threats. Fake videos made by deepfakes, false information generated by AI, biased worldviews created by algorithms—all have the power to collapse trust among people. The reconstruction of trust is one of the most urgent social tasks of the AI era.

Empathy capital is the social asset accumulated through the capacity for empathy. The memory of having been helped when in difficulty, the experience of having one's heart properly understood by someone, a history of overcoming hardship together—these form empathy capital. This capital, like money saved in a bank, is invisible, but it is the real power that lets a community endure together in a moment of crisis. If AI can raise efficiency and speed, empathy capital is the human's distinctive capacity for recovery that fills the social cracks AI has made.

Cultivating empathy capital at school is possible even without a special program. Truly listening to a friend's presentation, consciously including an alienated friend, listening first to each other's positions when conflict arises—these small practices build empathy capital. This becomes the foundation for making a truly humane organization later, when working alongside AI in society.

The advance of AI technology offers convenience, but at the same time it carries risk factors that can undermine social trust, such as the violation of personal information, algorithmic bias, and the spread of fake information. Therefore, in the AI era, it is important to reconstruct a healthy trust grounded in critical thinking rather than blind trust in technology. To this end, we must raise the transparency and explainability of AI systems, observe ethical principles in the process of AI development and use, and establish social oversight and regulation to prevent the misuse of technology. We must also accumulate "empathy capital" grounded in the human's distinctive capacity for empathy, and through it promote mutual understanding and cooperation to strengthen the foundation of social trust.

### 4.4. *Yokdae* (浴帶) and the Discernment of Good and Evil: The Final Line of Defense That Distinguishes AI from the Human

The human who has passed through "*yangsaeng*" in the Twelve Stages and come out into the world necessarily meets the stage of "*yokdae* (浴帶)." *Yokdae* literally means "to bathe and gird a sash," signifying—beyond merely covering the body—the establishment of an ethical identity that puts on the garment of social norms and begins to distinguish the good and evil (善惡) of the world.

This very character of "*yokdae*" is the core of the empathy at which Confucian Logos aims. Empathy is, beyond merely weeping together, the act of gravely judging what is right and what leads humanity to ruin (good and evil) within the web of relationships. Artificial intelligence (AI) can, on the basis of humanity's enormous data, "output" sad sentences in time with the sound of weeping. But because AI does not possess the actual body of suffering (*yangsaeng*), it cannot perform the process of "*yokdae* (the bone-deep embodiment of good and evil)"—of cleansing oneself and girding the ethical sash. In the coming age of extremes, the sole and most powerful real weapon that can distinguish and control the soulless machine algorithm from the human is precisely "the capacity to discern good and evil through empathy."

From the perspective of *hwajaeng*, the establishment of identity is not "choosing a single true self." Rather, it is acknowledging the self in its diverse forms while discovering a core value that does not waver in any situation. The I who laughs together with friends is I, the I who agonizes alone is I, and the I who receives AI's help is I; but what one regards as important when making a choice—that set of values is the true center of identity. Finding this center is the most important developmental task for young people in the AI era.

*Yokdae* (浴帶), in the Eastern stages of human development, signifies the period in which one takes one's first step into society and tests and establishes one's identity within relationships with others. The individual of the AI era must form their identity within a complex social environment where virtual and real are intermingled and diverse information and values collide. What matters in this process is forming social relationships through genuine empathy and communication with others, and finding one's role and meaning within the community. We must recognize that, while AI can be a tool for accessing information and communicating, genuine socialization and the establishment of identity are achieved through human interaction and experience.
